utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom. Mr. McCloskey, I saw you on your feet. Do you want to raise anything or is the next witness ready?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. The next witness is ready. This is the first time we've had a witness in this situation where he has been subpoenaed to be here. He is co-operative, he's here. I had a chance to speak to him about an hour ago very briefly, and there's very few exhibits I'll probably show him from that big list. There's one picture of the Borike Vila, which you'll recall from the site visit that he identified, that I've given a copy to Mr. Gajic, that I suggest we put on the ELMO for him to identify, but -- and it doesn't have any numbers, but I don't think it's anything that's contested. And Ms. Stewart may have it in the system by the time we get to that. Otherwise, we're ready to go. He is here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, the Prosecution has sent an e-mail yesterday with two additional documents which are not yet on the 65 ter exhibit list. Are you moving for admission of these and adding them to the 65 ter exhibit list?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. Based on our brief discussions with him today, it doesn't appear that that is something that is worthwhile, and I just sent that last night out of an abundance of caution in case it was something that he could speak to, and it doesn't appear that it is, so we don't need to cross that bridge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The witness should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, would you please stand for a moment. Please rise. First of all, welcome to the Tribunal. Good afternoon. Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card which is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your words of welcome. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And now please sit down and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now at the beginning of your testimony, the Prosecution is in the position to put questions to you. Mr. McCloskey, go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could you first just tell us your full name, and spell your last name so we get it correctly on the record.

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: My name is Djoko Razdoljac, R-a-z-d-o-l-j-a-c.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where were you born?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: I was born on the 13th of May, 1960, in Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what is your current line of work?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: I'm a trained economist employed in the agricultural complex AD Rogatica as a manager.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you give us just a brief biographical background. Where did you go to elementary/secondary school?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: I went to elementary school in Borike, I finished secondary school in Visegrad, and I got my university degree in Belgrade and Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when did you get your last university degree?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: My last university degree was three years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what was that in?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Well, in 1985, I graduated from the Higher School of Economics in Belgrade. Today, it's called the Higher School of Management. And I got my university degree in Economics in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Did you do regular JNA service at any point?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Yes, in 1983, 1984, in Svilajnac, Serbia. It was then still Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what job did you have during that service?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: I served my compulsory service in the Quarter-Master Service. There were cooks, bakers, butchers in my section. That's where I completed my training. And after the training, I served the rest of my compulsory service in hotels, in military hotels, on the Mountain of Tara as a soldier/waiter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And at some point, did you become a member of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: When the war started, of course I was in the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you just give us a brief summary when you first became a member of the VRS, and your first positions as we work our way to 1995. It doesn't need to be detailed. Just roughly.

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Towards the end of 1992, I started serving in the Command of Rogatica Brigade, until the end of 1995, and I was assistant commander for logistics all that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, then, let me go to 1995. Can you describe, in 1995, who -- as an assistant commander for logistics, who was your commander?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: My immediate superior was the commander of Rogatica Brigade, Rajko Kusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what rank was he in 1995, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: I think major or perhaps lieutenant-colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what rank were you in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Second lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you tell us what other assistant commanders were part of the Rogatica Brigade in July 1995, just so we can get a brief picture, a short picture of that command?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: We had Chief of Staff Milovan --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters ask the witness kindly to start over and say the name more slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir. They -- I think you're speaking rather softly, which is fine - the mikes are pretty good - but the interpreters didn't hear you. So could you tell us who the chief of staff -- who the chief of staff was again?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Lelek, Milovan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And his rank?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Captain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. The other assistants?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Assistant for security, Zoran Carkic. I think he was captain even then. Jadranko Vukovic, captain, was assistant for operations. Captain Miljan Djeric, captain first class. And myself, assistant for logistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you describe for us what the -- what your job entailed, especially in 1995. What was the assistant commander for logistics' duties?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Assistant commander for logistics is normally in charge of logistics. That involved providing food, equipment, munitions, fulfilling the requests of my superior command to the best of my ability.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you give us an example of a significant part of your job? I'm sure it involved, you know, supplying military supplies as well; weapons, ammunition, things like that. Didn't it?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Well, as instructed by the brigade, I filled out certain requests and submitted them to the Logistics Base of the 27th Brigade, or the logistical unit of the corps, or the staff, to a lesser extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. You've mentioned briefly these logistic bases. Can you explain to us how that worked? You said there was a corps logistics base. Would that have been the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you've also mentioned the 27th Logistics Base. What unit did that belong to?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: The 27th Logistics Base, I believe, belonged to both the Drina and the Sarajevo Corps and supplied them both.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was it at all associated with the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: The 27th Logistics Base was subordinate to both the corps and the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And you had a chance to speak briefly today with Investigator Tomasz Blaszczyk, did you not?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And I got to speak with you briefly as well today?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I just want to go over a couple of the things that I believe Mr. Blaszczyk may have gone over with you, and some of it should come up on the screen. The first one I would like to come up on the screen is P469. And to help simplify it, let me show you the original, which I think you may have had a chance to see. It's just a cardboard cover that the Court has seen before. It says "Telegram" on the front, "28/," it looks like, "34," perhaps "39," and then in Cyrillic, it says "Atlantida." And this was a cover page of various documents. Do you recall Mr. Blaszczyk showing you this cover page that said "Atlantida" on it?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you ever see this before? Do you ever recall seeing it before Mr. Blaszczyk showed it to you?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: No, I did not see this before nor was this present in my logistical base.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Does this term "Atlantida" have any significance for you? And I'm specifically referring back to the wartime period.

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: No. I saw that for the first time and came across this word for the first time when I met Mr. Tomasz Blaszczyk.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, let me just go over a couple of the documents that were found underneath this cardboard cover and just ask you a couple of questions about them. And they'll come up on the screen. The first one I'd like would be P471. Perhaps we can blow up the B/C/S a bit. That's a bit hard to read. Thank you, that's very good. Perhaps the same with the English. Now, I just want you to take a look at this. We see, in the left top corner, it says "27th POB Command." What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: That's the 27th Logistics Base.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that's what you spoke of earlier; correct?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then we see handwritten up in the right corner the numbers, it looks like, "330," and then the letters "Ziza." Does "Ziza" mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: It's the man who operated the teletype communications. His last name was Zizovic, and "Ziza" was short for it. He received and sent telegrams.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And this is -- as we see that it's dated 30 July 1995, and it's entitled "Report on War Booty," and it's to the 1st Podrinje "lpbr." Can you tell us what that is?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Light Podrinje Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what was that normally referred to, you know, among the members of that brigade, the name of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Rogatica Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And then as we go down, we see that it says: "Sjeversko Village IKM to PKPO personally." "IKM" is "Forward Command Post"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what is "PKPO"?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: To send the cable to the assistant commander for logistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And just to note, Your Honours, the translation says "assistant logistics commander." That's a bad translation. It should be as it was translated "assistant commander for logistics."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, this IKM in the Sjeversko village, do you recall that IKM?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And in what part of the village was it in?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: In the schoolhouse in the village of Sjeversko, which is in the central part of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And we see here that the body of this document says: "Please send us, according to our agreement of this evening, the data on the collected war booty so that we can carry out our obligation towards the VRS Main Staff." And then it is the assistant commander for logistics, Lieutenant-Colonel Strahinja Jankovic. Can you tell us who this Lieutenant-Colonel Jankovic is from the 27th Logistics Base Command?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who is that? Do you know him?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Well, I had to know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And this is -- as we've noted, it's to the assistant commander of the Rogatica Brigade personally. And who would have that been on 30 July 1995, the date this was sent?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Could you repeat that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Just going back up to who this was sent to, it says it was sent personally to the assistant commander for logistics to the 1st Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade. So who was that in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: That was me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell us here what the lieutenant-colonel is referring to when he says: "Please send us, according to our agreement of this evening, the data on collected war booty so that we can carry out our obligation towards the VRS Main Staff"? Do you remember the agreement -- an agreement you had with the lieutenant-colonel about war booty?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: There was an order to the effect that all war booty, meaning the cattle in the area of Zepa, should be pulled out or, rather, sent to the Rogatica Brigade, to the Borik Plateau, and from there, pursuant to other orders, they were to be taken in a vehicle of the 27th Logistics Base, and on orders from Mr. Strahinja, to the 27th Logistics Base, where it was then distributed on. Where to, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what is this obligation toward the Main Staff that he's referring to?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if they, too, distributed the cattle once it reached the 27th Logistics Base, so I don't really know whether the booty and the cattle -- the meat, actually, was then sent to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was there some kind of an agricultural farm in Sjemec, not far from Rogatica?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: There was a military -- well, actually, a farm, an agricultural farm there, except that in the Sjemec -- on the Sjemec Plateau, that farm belonged to the company that I work for today. And in the summertime, it was used for pasture for sheep and horses, because there is a very well-known horse stable at Borik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And was there any agricultural products being grown at that farm around Sjemec or the plain that you've referred to?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: No. Before the war, it was only pastures there. Now, after the war, they tried to start something else. They tried to sow -- to grow some wheat there, but that didn't work out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Really thinking about the summer, July/August, of 1995, do you know what kind of animals were -- if any, were stored at that farm at Sjemec?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: At that time, there was nothing at Sjemec. The horse stable and the sheep that were there, they remained on the Borik Plateau throughout the war. Now, only later, in 1995, when the war booty was pulled out from Zepa, the cows and calves were still kept at Borik Plateau, whereas the oxen, and I think there was some 100 or so of them, were at the Sjemec Plateau. And as I've already said, part of the booty was also sent to or towards the logistics base.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And so but that's the period after the fall of Zepa that you're talking about, correct, that the cattle and the other material got moved to Sjemec?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Well, yes. After the fall of Zepa, the cattle was driven from Zepa to Borike and Sjemec.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Right in that period right before or as Zepa was attacked - July 14th, I think, is the date that we've seen - were there any animals at the Sjemec farm in those big barns, big -- we've seen these big stone-foundation barns that were there on that plateau that you've described. At that period of time, were there any animals there?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Well, only the animals belonging to the locals from the Sjemec. Those people who had cattle, they used the pasture there, and their cattle was in the barns that were -- or stables that were left behind, empty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you give us just a very rough idea of how many head of cattle would have been there at that period of time in early July that the locals held?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: I really cannot do that. I don't know. I know that they had cattle, they had sheep, horses. But how many head of cattle, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did they have pigs?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: No. Pigs were not used for pasture -- grazing. They don't graze.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were any -- did you send any supplies -- any food, medicines, or anything like that to the Sjemec area for anyone, any humans, in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: To Sjemec? No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Roughly, how many people were living in that plateau? Just very roughly - I don't need exact numbers - in July 1995.

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Well, you see, at Sjemec, there was a plant of the forestry farm. I think there was some 10 to 15 houses there, or, rather, households of the local people. Now, how many people exactly, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you ever asked by anyone, your commander or anyone, whether or not Muslim prisoners could be accommodated anywhere in the Rogatica area before the fall of Zepa?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: No, not to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, specifically, did anyone ask you anything about sending 800 Muslims to the farm in Sjemec?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: No. No, there was no mention made in any version of Sjemec to accommodate those people nor did anyone talk about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was there agricultural work in the area of Sjemec for 800 people in early July 1995?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Well, no, no work needed to be done at Sjemec. As I've already said, there was just some cattle there, grazing on the pastures, but there was no farm work to be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to another -- a document. This is P472. And that should come up, and we'll blow that up for you as well, because this is handwritten.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, we can see, from the -- from this document, that up in the right-hand corner it's dated 30 July 1995 at 1640 hours. Can you make out that handwriting? Do you recognise that handwriting at all, any of it?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: I can only recognise my own signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And could you -- there's a way to mark on this -- on this machine, and I think the Usher will help you. If you could -- he'll show you where this marker pen is, and you can actually draw right on the screen and it will leave a mark. So could you circle where you see your signature?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay, you've circled that in red. Do you see your name spelled out anywhere else?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Well, at the very beginning, in the heading, I can see, in the upper left corner, my first and last name, although that's not in my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Could you underline that so we know what you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, you've circled it. So could you put a "2" next to that circle so we'll be able to distinguish the two circles.

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. So that "2" is next to your name spelled out by someone else; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you make out the name over on the right-hand side? It's under "1640 hours," or the word, whatever that is? I know it's difficult, but perhaps --

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And is this one of the documents Mr. Blaszczyk showed you today, earlier?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did he show you an original document?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: No, I saw this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let me see if I can get you the original. If I could hand you a document containing the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: With the assistance of the Court Usher, it should be given to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, this looks to me like it's ink. Is that a copy of what we see on the screen or is it the same as what we see on the screen, as far as you can tell?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Well, as far as I can tell, it should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And looking at that, what I'll refer to as the original, is that your signature at the bottom, just like it is on the copy on the screen?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you sign that?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you remember this document at all?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Well, it's been a long time. I can't really recall this document, but the signature is mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So is this a genuine document?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I don't know what you mean. Do you mean has someone falsified this document that I'm holding?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Does it look falsified to you in any way?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Well, I think that the person who sent this was probably in the field somewhere and that it was actually sent by courier to me, which is why it was handwritten.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Any doubt that that's your signature at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: No, no, this is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I think we're done, though -- and these are all in evidence already, I believe, but let me check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Not with the markings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But not with the markings, absolutely. So I best offer this document with the markings. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The marked document will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The marked version of document P00472 shall be given Exhibit P01432. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, did Mr. Blaszczyk show you some video-clips of the wartime period around -- I think it was around the Borike/Boksanica area today?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Yes, Borik and Boksanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And were you able to see yourself in some of those clips, and some other folks?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Yes, at Boksanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And just to try to make it as clear as possible: In looking at -- there's a short note of the information you gave Mr. Blaszczyk. Did he read that note over to you, and did you make sure it was correct?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Yes, he read it out to me, and I just confirmed that that's what I had said, as it was written down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay, thanks. Let me just read briefly a couple of sections to make sure we've got this right. It says, in paragraph 3, that: "Mr. Razdoljac was shown a portion of the videos 8119 and 1355." And on 1355, you identified yourself, Hamdija Torlak, Benjamin Kulovac, General Mladic, General Tolimir, Colonel Dudnjik of the Ukrainian Battalion, at a meeting at Boksanica on 19th of July? So is that correct? You saw the video of that meeting on 19th, and you were able to identify those people?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Yes, within the UNPROFOR compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that was -- where was that?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: That was at Boksanica, at the UNPROFOR compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And then it says on Video 8119 you were able to identify yourself greeting General Mladic when he had arrived to Boksanica by helicopter on 26th July 1995; that you also identified Jadranko Vukovic from the Rogatica Brigade, Mladic's bodyguards, and Strahinja Jankovic from the 27th Logistic Base, and General Zdravko Tolimir and General Milan Gvero. Is that correct, you were able to do that from that video-clip?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How did you know it was 26th July?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't really know nor did I say at any point that it was on the 26th of July. I know that the Zepa operation was toward the end of July 1995, but what date exactly it was, I really don't know, because there were events every day. And even if I did know the date at the time, I wouldn't have been able to remember them all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So that 26th July date would have been something supplied to you by Mr. Blaszczyk?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Yes, he said it was a video-clip of the 26th. Now, I never said that it was either the 25th, or the 26th, or the 10th, for that matter. I only said who I could identify on the video-clip. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And is that the same for the video-clip from the 19th, that he told you this was a video-clip from the 19th and you were able to identify those people?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Well, I stand by what I've already said. I identified the people, but as for the date, I could not really confirm that because all of this was happening during Operation Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. During that Operation Zepa in July 1995, where was General Tolimir staying?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: I had occasion to see General Tolimir at Boksanica, and I also saw him at Borike.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where did you see him at Borike?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Well, in Borike, there was a building next to the hotel that was some sort of forward command post, and sometimes people would stay overnight there during Operation Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what was this commonly referred to, this building?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: It was referred to as the Vila.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where was it in relation to the hotel building in Borike?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: It was east of the hotel, some 100 metres away, maybe 150.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Could we put 65 ter 7001 on the screen. It may take a while to show up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But do you remember, did Mr. Blaszczyk show you a photograph of a building today?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He showed me the photograph of that Vila.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And were you able to identify the photograph yourself?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And now we have a photograph, with snow, of a building. What is this building on this photograph, 65 ter 7001?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: This is the building that we referred to as Vila in Borike.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how was it that you saw General Tolimir there at some point during the Zepa operation? What was it for?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Well, the centre was in Boksanica. There were a lot of people there, it was crowded. There were media representatives. There were also people from the superior commands. And one evening, I believe they were to spend the night there, but there were only four bedrooms in that Vila, and I vividly recall that it was very crowded, there were lots of people there, and they were looking for extra rooms. And on that night, General Mladic was there, too, and that's when General Tolimir was there, that I saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who got the four bedrooms that night?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I know that I didn't get one. I had to go back, because my superiors were there from the Main Staff, and there were also reporters from various media outlets. And I remember there was a woman, and Mladic intervened for her to be provided with accommodations, and I remember that Mladic criticised me because I wasn't very forthcoming.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What do you mean? Forthcoming about what?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You said General Mladic criticised you because you weren't forthcoming. Can you explain what you meant by that? What were you not forthcoming about?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Well, he asked me to provide the rooms for all of them, and I just told him, Well, General, there are only four bedrooms here, I really cannot do anything about it. And that is when he said, Well, all right. Then if I, General Mladic, have to sleep under a tree, I'll do so, but I want you to make sure that this lady gets or be provided proper accommodation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who was this woman?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: It wasn't only one woman; there were several. I don't know who exactly he meant. There were several people from the media. I only know that later BBC and Sky News reported about it. Whether there were any reporters from Serbia or elsewhere, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who was staying in the hotel rooms in the nearby hotel, which we know has several rooms, at that evening that you were there during the Zepa operation?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Well, at the time the hotel was not really properly outfitted, and I think that only the assistant commander for logistics of the battalion that was there was able to sleep there, and perhaps a driver who had to spend the night there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You mentioned to Mr. Blaszczyk that, and I quote: "He recalls that General Zdravko Tolimir used this Vila during the Zepa operation in July 1995." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Well, I said that all those who -- all of us who were in Boksanica went to the Vila when necessary, whether to attend a meeting or to spend the night there, and that was a reference to all of us whom I saw or who could be seen there in Boksanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You clearly had to look after the logistics of these generals. So did General Tolimir spend the night at this Vila any time during the Zepa operation?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Possibly. He could have spent a few nights there. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Where else could he have or did he spend the night during the Zepa operation, which we know went on -- well, we know from the 13th of July near to the end of July. Where else would or did General Tolimir spend the night when he was in the area of Boksanica/Borike/Rogatica?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: I don't know if he could have slept at the Rogatica Command or perhaps a few nights in the trenches at Boksanica. I don't know whether he went to the Main Staff. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How long a drive was it, during that wartime period from, say, the Vila to Crna Rijeka, the Main Staff headquarters?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: That all depends on which route you take. If you go through Borike, Rogatica, Sokolac, Han Pijesak, it takes 90 minutes to 2 hours. And if you took a shortcut, Budeta-Mrkalji-Han Pijesak, then he would have there within an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So this shortcut in July, during the operation, was there anything to prevent him from taking the shortcut if he had, you know, a decent vehicle and ...

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: I don't know what there could have been to prevent him. It was very deep behind our lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you describe -- going back to the Vila, what kind of communications, if any, did that Vila have with the outside?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Yes, there was a radio communications room next to the Vila.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Where was the radio communications room?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: I think it was the largest room downstairs, or perhaps a lounge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In what building?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Which building? It's only one building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, we're talking about the radio communication is in the Vila, the hotel, the Sjeversko School, some out-building? Which building? I'm sorry, we may have gotten a bit confused.

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: I said a moment ago that the hotel was used only by the logistics man in the battalion. He had communications, and there was a communications line to Sjeversko, the battalion command, and there was a communications unit in the Vila. That was in the conference room. Perhaps that should be the best name for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's start with the Vila. What kind of communications did the Vila have to the hotel communication that you just described?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: The same communications, radio communications. The hotel was linked up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was there a hard line from the Vila to the hotel?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: The cable, the wire cable for radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's correct. Can you describe that to us?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: How shall I describe it? The grey military cable stretched to connect these features, attached to trees, from one fir tree to another. You can see it was in a forest, and from the hotel a cable was laid through the forest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So was the cable laid through the forest from the hotel communications room to the Vila?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: I think one line came straight to the hotel, and another went under the hotel to the Vila.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so the Vila, itself, did it have just one of those induction telephone things or did it have actual radio equipment with a receiver and a transmitter?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: The switchboard for that radio station was at Borike, in the old building of the local office. And from there, a line went to Sjeversko, connecting both the hotel and the Vila.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So the Vila, the hotel, the Sjeversko School, were all connected with a central communications centre in an old building?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And where -- can you describe this old building to us so we can get a picture of what it was?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: It was the local office of the registry before the war. That was levelled before the war, and a new building was built where nowadays the president of the Local Commune and the registrar are located.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you tell us -- you must have some basic knowledge of the radio, since you had to provide supplies. What kind of radio receiver and transmitter was it? We've heard about RUP 12s, RRU 2s, lots of others that I can't -- well, a couple of others that I can't remember now. Can you tell us what was there at that -- at that building?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: I honestly don't know. Whatever I say, I may be wrong. I honestly never went inside that building, not once. That's where these young men who operated the communications worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, did you use those -- take advantage of those communications yourself, like get on the phone at the hotel or at the Vila?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: No, no. My office was in Rogatica, and as long as the Zepa operation lasted, I was in Boksanica, sometimes sleeping in the trenches, or I commuted to Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you remember a hard line being pulled out on the 13th -- or taken out on the 13th to the Boksanica check-point?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: I don't know what date it was, but in the trench-line in Boksanica there was a line, if not in all trenches. I think all the trenches were connected by a cable.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The area around the Ukrainian Check-Point 2, I think you referred to it as, do you remember that, Check-Point 2 at Boksanica, where the Ukrainian Battalion was?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: I don't know which check-point it was or which number it was, but I knew it, and all of us called it the UNPROFOR at Boksanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And was there a hard line run from that area to Borike as the operation for Zepa came underway?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I know we had some communications at Boksanica, but I don't know whether it was that hard line or something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let me -- I think we'll play a bit of the video. I'm not sure we need to play it all, but let me just -- we have a little bit more time left, so let's start with what we have -- what has been identified to you as 19 July, Mladic arriving by helicopter. And that is 65 -- sorry, P00740. Okay, and we'll -- well, we'll start it at -- the counter is "00:02:50.1." And I may ask you a few questions about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just to start with, do you recognise this meadow and this tree area?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: It's Boksanica, the broader view at Boksanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. We're at 00:03:07.5.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think we all will agree that's General Mladic on the left. How about the person in the middle; who's that?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: That's me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how about the person on the far right?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: That's assistant commander for moral issues, Captain Jadranko Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And why were you there to greet General Mladic that day?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: I was not with General Mladic that day. My orders were to go there and to do this and that, and when Mladic landed at Boksanica, he asked after the commander, he was told the commander was not there, and he told me, You, bloke, will go to the meeting with me, and you will be representing the Rogatica Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I understand, sir, but can you give us a little more detail? We know that -- and I know you didn't mean this, but your orders certainly weren't to "do this and that." Do you recall, specifically, what your orders were, or even just generally what your orders were?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: On that day or in general?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: On that day, prior to you meeting General Mladic briefly here in this field.

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: On that day, I did not have any particular orders from General Mladic, except to be present, which you will probably see later, at that meeting, at the negotiations. And one more thing, I'm sorry. Captain Vukovic was supposed to go, but he was not clean-shaven, and General Mladic gave him three minutes to get ready. That's why he did not attend the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Can you tell us what orders you had received from your command that morning for this day? Surely, you received orders from your command the day that Mladic is coming.

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Well, my only order was to be at Boksanica during those days and to carry out preparations - I don't know if you have that footage - preparations for the evacuation of people from Zepa and those buses and lorries that arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's just continue to play.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So the fellow with the blue helmet, who's that?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: I believe that's Dudnjik of UNPROFOR, commander. If he takes off the helmet, I'll be sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's continue to play.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just one question here. We're at 00:03:47.1. Do you recognise this little room where General Mladic is sitting and this guy with, it looks like, a blue beret?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: I have never been in this room. And this man looks like Rajko Kusic. I'm not sure it's him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry. Which one looks like Rajko Kusic?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: This man sitting next to General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How about the man standing; do you recognise him?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: That's Dudnjik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Okay, let's go to another section. We still believe that this is the 19th, and we begin at 00:28:30.0.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. We've stopped at 00:29:32.5, and we've panned to the end of the table.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us, if you know, who the fellow -- the balding fellow with the big moustache on the left side of the screen is?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: No, I don't know that man.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Have you heard of a man named Lieutenant-Colonel Svetozar Kosoric, intel officer with the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So do you know if you've ever met Lieutenant-Colonel Kosoric?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: If that's him --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry. I was just asking you if you'd ever met Lieutenant-Colonel Kosoric before. You said you've heard of him. Had you ever met him before?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And I know this view isn't very good. Were you at this table at this time; do you remember? Let's continue to watch it. Maybe it will get clearer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Indiscernible] there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Is that you right in the front of the screen at 00:20:42.3, the profile?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry. "00:29," sorry. And the other person who we see across the table from you, who's that?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: That's this Dudnjik from the Ukrainian Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's play a little more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Stopping at 00:29:55.3, we can just see that you were taking notes. Do you remember what you were taking notes about and why?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Well, I got orders from General Mladic to keep a record, to take notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what was going on here, just briefly?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Negotiations were about the voluntary departure of Muslims from Zepa, and this is one of the rounds of negotiations where I attended. There were others that I did not attend. And all these negotiations resulted, as you will later probably show, in the evacuation of the people from Zepa using this route Boksanica-Rogatica towards Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I can see it's break time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed. Thank you very much, Mr. McCloskey. We must have our first break now. The Court Usher will assist you during the break. We will resume at quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I had inadvertently forgotten to offer 65 ter 7001, the picture of the Vila, into evidence. So if I could do that now, I'd appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Only for a better understanding, is this already on the 65 ter exhibit list?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, that was not something I did discuss with Mr. Gajic, and -- we had talked about it. He didn't have a problem. It was something the witness just identified in proofing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And I don't see any objection by the Defence. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Leave is granted to add it to the 65 ter exhibit list, and it will be received. But I would like to -- yes, first the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P01433, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could that be played again and so that we can see it on the screen. Not the video-clip but the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: 65 ter 7001, and the number, of course, you just gave it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We have it on the screen now. I'd like to put one question to the witness about this photograph. On the left, the bottom side of this picture, there is handwriting. Can you tell us about that, with the date of the 30th of November, 2010?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is my signature that I affixed to this photograph today, and I said that this was at the Vila at Borike. And I did this in Mr. Tomasz' office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That was just for clarification. Please continue, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And we also -- it just said "attached as exhibit," so that photograph was attached to his brief statement of this morning. So that's what that other handwriting was about. Okay. I think we can just continue a bit more of this video-clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. We're stopping at 00:30:08.1, and I think that's -- I don't have any further questions, I think we've basically done what we need to. And if we could go to the next one, which is, we believe, 26 July, Boksanica. Same number, and, yeah, that's P00740. We're starting at 00:37:30.0.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just stopping at 00:37:50.8, do you recognise the man in the uniform on the left side of the screen?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who is that?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you know the man that he's shaking hands with? Do you know who that is?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Have you ever seen or met the commander of the Zepa Brigade, Avdo Palic?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was he ever in custody in the Rogatica Brigade anywhere after the Zepa population was transported out?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: As far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who's responsible for providing supplies and logistics to the prison facility in Rogatica?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: It was my Quarter-Master Service.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you aware of any Muslims from Zepa being held there after the population was transported out in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: After Zepa, I'm not aware that there were any people from Zepa held in custody. As far as I knew, all these buses, and there were many of them, had gone through Rogatica and on to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was there a detention facility in Rogatica in July 1995 that the military used?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Not in July. But during the war years, there was a detention facility in Luznica. That's on the outskirts of Rogatica -- or, rather, as one was going into Rogatica from Sarajevo, it was on the left-hand side of the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What's it being used currently for now?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Now, at that location, there are sawmills, privately-owned sawmills that process timber.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, perhaps it -- I know it was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, a small clarification, because the last reply that the witness gave was not fully interpreted, perhaps because of the term -- of a term that the witness used that is difficult to interpret into English. So we would appreciate it if Mr. McCloskey could put the question to the witness again, and perhaps the witness can give a simpler answer, using simpler terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, would you like to do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us, as simply as you can, what that prison facility that was used during the war is currently being used for?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: That site had several facilities. Those facilities have been sold to private entrepreneurs who now use them mainly for processing timber and timber products.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, I know it's been a long time, but there have been -- there's, well, been at least one witness, there are other witnesses, there are documents. It's very clear that in July 1995, that men from Zepa were being held at this place you've described, and they were eventually turned over -- some of them were turned over to the Red Cross and lived to come testify here. In thinking about that now, do you think you may have mis-recollected that?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: No, I stand by what I have said. I had -- I have no information that there were people held in custody there. What I know is that we had loyal people there from Okrugli and Satorovici who stayed there for a while. As for people from Zepa being held in custody, I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, one of the documents I spoke to you earlier about that I had put on the list -- actually, you asked me about it, that I said I hadn't intended to use it, and I hadn't. But the witness has just provided me with an answer to a question that I would like to use the document to refresh his recollection, to see if it will refresh his recollection on this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Which one is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It has been given the number of 6870.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I take it this is not yet in the 65 ter exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's correct. This is a document that we have recently received. And as soon as we got it, we gave it to the Defence. I think it was a few weeks ago, though Ms. Stewart will correct me on that if I'm -- if I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, Mr. Gajic, what is the position of the Defence, using this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, bear with me for a moment, please. The Defence has no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Then the document will be added to the 65 ter exhibit list, and you may use it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. And that -- if we could bring that up on the screen. But I also have a hard copy that I would like to give the witness, because it's multi pages and I think it will be easier for him to take a look at it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: With the assistance of the Court Usher, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And please take your time, take a look at it. It will come up on the screen in both languages here in a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could we have that document on the screen, please. We don't have it yet. Now I think we see it on the screen. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll just note, as we can slowly go through this document, that it is from the Command of the Rogatica Brigade, the Organ for Security and Intelligence, dated 30 July. General Miletic's name is written on the top of it. It is from Captain Zoran Carkic, the chief of the security organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you remind us who Carkic is, sir?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: As I've already mentioned, Mr. Zoran Carkic was the assistant for security in the Rogatica Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And he sends this to the -- as we see from the first page, the Main Staff, Sector for Intel and Security, and the Security Administration, and to the Command of the Drina Corps. And it's entitled "Regarding an A, information about rz ..." Is "rz" "prisoners of war"?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: "... in the Holding Centre, Rogatica." Then it reads: "Since July 28, 1995, the following Muslims have a status of prisoners of war, placed in the military holding centre in Rogatica." The first one is "Mehmed Hajric," noted to be the president of the War Presidency of Zepa and a hodja by profession. Number 2 is "Hamdija Torlak," the former president of the Municipal Executive Board, an electrical engineer. The third is "Amir Imamovic," former commander of the Civil Protection Staff. And then it goes on. I won't name everyone. It lists several other folks. I get to number 45. It's page -- well, yeah, page 3 in the English. Page 2 is just a list of names as well. Page 2 in the B/C/S. Number 45 is, we hear this word again, "Atlantida," "1958, in a safe place and at another location." What does this word "Atlantida" mean, anyway, just by itself, not as a code-name or anything, but what does it mean to you, "Atlantida"?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: To me, personally, it doesn't mean anything. This is the first time that I come across the word, "Atlantida."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is it -- I don't know if it's the fictional island that we grew up in school about that disappeared under the ocean. Does that ring any bells?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: No, it doesn't mean a thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And were you ever aware that Avdo Palic was a prisoner and given a code-name?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And then as we go to page 4 in the English, it talks about the Muslim prisoners being treated - page 3 in the B/C/S - and their situation. It says: "Atlantida is a picture of health." We go to page 5 in the English, and on the top of the page it says: "Pursuant to the orders and instructions of General Tolimir, all the necessary measures are taken and in accordance to the possibility they are mainly being carried out. Among other things, the following was done:" And it talks about organising the prisoners in three different rooms according to their -- wounded and sick in one room, members of the former leadership in another room, and the healthy in another room. It says: "Atlantida is separated and placed in another location and has better accommodation. "The effendi is allowed to pray in a room five times a day. "They have food (three times a day) - they use the outhouse. "They have medical treatment. "On 30 July this year, they are visited and registered by the ICRC delegation office at Pale." So we can see from this document there appears to be prisoners held in Rogatica at a site, and General Tolimir has issued orders looking after them. And it goes on to talk about the evacuation of the civilian population from Zepa. And then at the end, some of the Muslim men complained to General Tolimir that money had been taken by the people separating them, and General Tolimir demanded that the case of the stolen money be investigated. That's page 6 in the English. Carkic writes this under the authority -- under the authorisation of General Tolimir. Surely, does this help you refresh your recollection about the men who were being held at Rogatica and being taken care of?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could Mr. McCloskey please point out where he found that I issued the order to Carkic to write this down, because that's what he said in the transcript, or perhaps he should rephrase his question to actually be in sync with the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We must just have a translation issue. I was pretty much quoting the document and noting the pages. I would go to the last page and the last paragraph, where it says, right after I said that General Tolimir demanded that this stolen money be investigated, it says that Carkic wrote this, and I quote, "by authorisation from General Tolimir." I'm not sure how that was translated to you, but that is those last three lines in B/C/S, and I quote: "By authorisation from General Tolimir. "Chief of the Intelligence and Security Organ, Captain Zoran Carkic." That should be the exact translation, so I hope that helps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So, sir, this is one of many records indicating that there was prisoners there, most of whom were -- survived. Does this help refresh your recollection about Muslims being held in Rogatica at that facility that is now used as a lumber facility?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: This is news to me, that such a large number of people from Zepa were here. I don't know for how many days you are saying they were detained. But after the end of Operation Zepa, I spent about 10 days in Zepa. I had a forward command post for logistics in the center of Zepa, and we stayed there until the evacuation of all livestock was finalised from the entire territory of Zepa. So I really don't know about this. All this is the responsibility of the Security Sector. I had no responsibility whatsoever concerning prisons or detention centres or prisoners. Our only role was to provide food for the prison, and I have to stress that there were both Serbs and Muslim soldiers in the prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So there were Muslim prisoners in the prison in Rogatica as well as Serbs; is that what you're saying now?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Yes. As Muslims were detained, Serb soldiers were kept there too. It was the same building, different rooms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you called on to provide any logistic support for the securing, transporting, killing and burying of Mehmed Hajric, number 1 on the list, Amir Imamovic, number 3 on the list, or Avdo Palic?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: No, no. As far as these specific people are concerned, I was never told they were in prison nor was any logistical support concerning them ever asked for.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You were in Zepa for several days after the fall of Zepa. Can you tell us what happened to the mosque that was standing in Zepa after all the Muslims left?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Blown up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Under whose orders?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: I wouldn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How do you know it was blown up?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Because, as I said before, I was in Zepa after the operation, and I was there with other people from logistics and transport, and I looked -- I watched that detail from an elevation when the mosque was blown up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I think there could be a reason for giving a caution to the witness at this point in time, pursuant to Rule 90(E) of our Rules of Procedure and Evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think you're absolutely correct, Mr. President, and I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, I would like to give you some guidance, Mr. Razdoljac. You know you were asked quite a lot of questions. They are very difficult for you, but I have to give you some guidance. We have, in our Rules of Procedure and Evidence, the Rule 90(E), and I would like to read it out for you. And I quote: "A witness may object to making any statement which might tend to incriminate the witness. The Chamber may, however, compel the witness to answer the question. Testimony compelled in this way shall not be used as evidence in a subsequent prosecution against the witness for any offence other than false testimony." Did you understand what I was reading to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Mr. McCloskey, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you saw the mosque get blown up?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So what kind of explosion -- what explosives were used?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: I don't know. I was not on that team. If you were listening, I said I had watched that from an elevation. There was a team that came from outside because we did not have these explosives experts, as they call them, in our brigade. I'm not sure, but I heard later that a lot of anti-tank mines were laid there. I don't know if there's any connection with the blowing up of the mosque, all I know is that it was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How many people were in the unit that destroyed it, that you saw?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Five or six, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what kind of vehicle did they have?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: I really don't know. There was a military vehicle of some sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And were they in uniform?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were they Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were they army forces?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Of course. As long as they were uniformed, they were members of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In your opinion, as an assistant commander for logistics throughout the war, could that mosque have been blown up by that army unit without the knowledge of the chief of intelligence and security of the Main Staff, Zdravko Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: I don't know that. I don't know who knew about it or who gave the orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The houses around the town were destroyed as well, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: In Rogatica?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Zepa.

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: In Zepa? Zepa is not a town. Zepa has always been a village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: At about the same time the mosque was blown up, were there houses around the village of Zepa destroyed as well?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: No. On that day when the mosque was blown up, it was just the mosque. These young men, the sappers, just did that job, as we say, and then left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, in the days after that or before that, were houses around the Zepa village destroyed by fire or by explosives? And, sir, I can tell you I have a photograph.

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: I don't know what you have, but the houses that were destroyed in Zepa, I think, were burned. The mosque was the only thing that was blown up, to the best of my knowledge and from all I saw, because while I was there in Zepa, after the Operation Zepa was finished, in the schoolhouse not 100 metres away from me, the UNPROFOR was based, and I remember very clearly three or four days later, after the army moved through Zepa, an old Muslim woman showed up suddenly, and I turned her over to the UNPROFOR to be shipped to Sarajevo. The only thing she asked for was a cigarette, and she was sitting on the threshold in the courtyard of the mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So the houses that we're talking about, you've acknowledged on line 9: "But the houses --" and I'm quoting you "-- that were destroyed in Zepa, I think, were burned." Yes. And who burned them?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Well, probably the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us -- you've grown up in Rogatica, I'm sure you had Muslim friends, you probably still do. How important is the village mosque to a Muslim in their culture and their identity?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Well, it's probably as important as the church is to us Orthodox Christians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And tell us how important the church is, then, so we know both.

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Well, if you ask to what extent, every place of worship is very important to every nation, every people, every community. That's where you pray to God.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, sir. I don't have any other questions. And, Your Honour, regarding this document - it's 6870 - because it is relatively new and we could provide much more information, I would only offer it at this time if the General Tolimir would offer it with me. Otherwise, I would provide you with more detail and more information about where it came from and how it came to us, and give the Defence more time to look at it themselves. If he wishes to offer it with us, we will offer it now for you. If not, I will hold off on that and provide you more evidence about it, which we will, of course, do anyway. But that is my offer to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is a fair proposition. Mr. Tolimir, what is your position?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I greet everyone present. I hope that this hearing and the whole trial will be completed in keeping with God's will, not necessarily mine. I do not object to the admission of this document regarding Zepa and the events in Zepa. I don't mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In that event, I do offer this into evidence, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P01434, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And we are waiting for some additional clarification about what you proposed and how you received this document at a later stage of this trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Absolutely, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Nyambe has a question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. In fact, I have three clarifications that I hope you can give me. At page 6, line -- at page 6 of today's transcript, lines 12 to 13, you are recorded as having said the following, that: "The 27th Logistics Base, I believe, belonged to both the Drina and the Sarajevo Corps, and I supplied them both." Can you just clarify that for me, especially with regard to the fact that you supplied them both, and what the relationship is between the two, the Sarajevo Corps and the Drina Corps. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that's not exactly what I said. I think there must be a misunderstanding. I was not with the 27th Logistics Brigade. I was assistant commander for logistics in the Rogatica Brigade. 27th is the number of the logistics base that was supposed to provide logistical support both to the Sarajevo Corps and the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you. So then what is the relationship between the Drina Corps and the Sarajevo Corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What kind of relationship? A good relationship. In the beginning of the war, the first year or two of the war, the Rogatica Brigade belonged to the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, and later, by virtue of some order, it was attached to the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you. My second question relates to -- you must forgive me. I'm trying to understand the complete context in which these events occurred. At page 32, lines 6 to 9, you have referred to during the war years, there was a detention facility in a place. Which war years are you referring to here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From early 1993 until the signing of the Dayton Accords, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you. I have one more question for you. At page 42, lines 3 to 4, you have referred -- in answering a question from the Prosecution, you referred to: "These young men, these sappers, just did that job, as we say, and then left." Who are the sappers? Can you just give me a little bit of more explanation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The sappers, s-a-p-p-e-r-s, belonged to the VRS. And from where exactly they came, on whose orders, I don't know. I did not have any contact with them nor did I provide them with logistical support for this action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your explanations.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now Mr. Tolimir has the right to cross-examine you, and you will be asked to answer his questions. Mr. Tolimir, please commence your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon again to everyone. Good afternoon to the witness. I hope he has a pleasant stay with us and a good return home, with God's blessings.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, let's start from the end, to make it easier for you. Do you know when the evacuation of Zepa was completed and when all the activities in Zepa were finalised?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: It lasted for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I have to -- I thought we didn't receive interpretation. Therefore, I stopped you. But you may continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said I don't know exactly when the evacuation was completed, but it took several days. I know what my task was within it, where I participated in securing 50 to 60 buses and lorries that carried the people being evacuated from Zepa, and the support in the travel over bad roads towards Boksanica, and that involved the assistance from us who were in Boksanica and assistance from the UNPROFOR. People moved over to buses, and then a convoy was formed which travelled, as far as I know, to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
