utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the e-court display 1D -- sorry, no, D55, page 32, paragraph 114. That's the page before in English. Thank you, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is paragraph 114. I will read it out to remind you of these events, and then I'll ask my question. At --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, could you please indicate which kind of document you are reading from. What is it about? We didn't receive a list of documents to be used during the cross-examination. That is the reason why I asked for that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the document called "The Fall of Zepa," a report on the military events, prepared for the OTP by Mr. Bezruchenko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I quote paragraph 114: "At 2345 hours on 27 July, the last convoy with 325 displaced persons left Zepa for Kladanj, while the VRS made another ultimatum to BiH soldiers to lay down their arms by 0800 hours on 28th July. At 1015 on 29 July, the UNPROFOR liaison team reported that the evacuation was completed and that control was being established over isolated villages in the pocket. General Mladic and UNPROFOR commander General Smith held a meeting in the early afternoon." Now, concerning these activities that I read about on the 27th and 28th July, do you remember where you were at the time and if you were in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: During the evacuation, and this text says that the evacuation was taking place on those days, I was at Boksanica. As I said before, I don't know the exact dates, but I did not go down into Zepa until it was practically clean; that is to say, until the VRS had moved to the Zepa Mountain. Only when the VRS was on Zepa Mountain did we get the orders to go down into Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Tell us, for the record, what date was it, approximately, when the army moved to Mount Zepa? Because the Trial Chamber does not know, and they will have to make a judgement about our activities on that basis.

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: When the army moved to Mount Zepa, in July/early August, I think. I don't know. You really shouldn't try to pin me down to particular dates, because the time has done its work.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now display paragraph 117. There it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'll quote the first three lines: "The commander of the 285th Brigade, Avdo Palic, was in VRS custody on 28th July because General Tolimir had reported that the 285th Brigade commander, Avdo Palic, had supplied information on minefields in the area of Zepa." Is it obvious from this document that General Tolimir did not hide the fact that Avdo Palic was in detention, in the custody of the VRS? On the contrary, he said specifically that Avdo Palic had provided information about minefields.

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: I don't know if you were hiding it or not. I said all I could say about Avdo Palic. I did not meet him, and I don't know what was going on with him at that time, and I don't know that he was in detention.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: But if somebody makes a written report, saying that somebody is in detention and that this person had provided information about minefields, does the writer of such a report hide the fact that this person is in detention, or is it, on the contrary, an action of transparency?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Of course it's transparent. You can see that there's -- no one's making any bones about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you remember when it was that you saw this mosque being blown up in Zepa, as you talked about it a little earlier?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact day, but I know it was sometime in the morning, around 10.00 or 11.00, that that was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you remember whether you saw any officers from the Main Staff in Zepa at the time?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: No. I am 100 per cent sure that no one was there, no officers, because the forward command post was near the mosque and they were called out -- we were called and told that we should withdraw. And we went up there to that elevation, and me and my men, we just stood there and watched what was happening without a word.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. McCloskey asked you whether the mosque could have been blown up without the knowledge of General Tolimir. Now, could you tell me, please, whether you saw General Tolimir there, where your forward command post was in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Well, I state with full responsibility that on that day General Tolimir was not in Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know whether General Tolimir was in Zepa on the 30th, after the civilians were evacuated? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: I don't think you were there after the evacuation of the population. I don't think you were in Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We saw a little earlier that the evacuation was concluded on the 28th. We quoted paragraph 114. Now can we take a look at paragraph 119. In Serbian, that's on the next page. We see 119 in English before us, and that's on the next page in Serbian. And it says there, and I quote paragraph 119: "An UNPROFOR Civil Affairs report is broadly consistent with the UNPROFOR report dated 28th of July." And then they go on and speak about: "The forced cleansing of women, children and elderly in 20 buses provided by the Serbs was carried out, if not with dignity at least with UNPROFOR escorts and without the same large-scale abuses of human rights as occurred in Srebrenica. However, in one case, two women were said to have been forcibly removed from a bus by Serb soldiers in unclear circumstances. By 28th July, 4.336 civilians, including 197 wounded, had left Zepa and been transported to BH territory." Thank you. My question now. Since UNPROFOR confirmed in its report the description of the evacuation in Zepa, and they also mentioned this incident with the removal of the two women from the bus, is it clear, from what it states here, that the evacuation was conducted on the 28th of July, as it says in the report there? Is this, in fact, a report of the 28th of July?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: I'm not clear what you mean by your question, if that was a question for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please take a look at paragraph 119, line 2. Is this report, provided by the UNPROFOR, dated the 28th of July, which I quoted, where they described the manner in which people from Zepa were evacuated? Would you please take a look at the date. When is -- what is the date on that report? Could you please tell us? That's in paragraph 119. I will repeat my question. What is the date of this report by UNPROFOR that I quoted a moment ago in paragraph 119?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Are you asking me to comment on paragraph 119 with -- where it says, "The forced cleansing of women, children, and the elderly," and so on?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: No, no, no, that's not what I'm asking you to do. I'm just asking you whether this report is from the 28th of July, this UNPROFOR report, because it says here that this report is broadly consistent with UNPROFOR report dated the 28th July. So have I quoted that correctly, the report that is mentioned in paragraph 119? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Well, if you're asking me about the date, I really don't know whether it was, in fact, on that date, as stated in the UNPROFOR report. I'm a bit confused by your question --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, I quoted an UNPROFOR report, a document where an UNPROFOR report is quoted, and all I'm asking you is whether this is in fact an UNPROFOR report of 28th of July.

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Well, that's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, that's all I wanted you to confirm, because you said you couldn't remember the date when the mosque was blown up. So I just want to place this in some kind of time-frame. Now, could you please take a look at paragraph 124. We'll see that it says in paragraph 124 the following: "On 21st July, UNPROFOR in Zepa reported that VRS was burning houses in the town and nearby villages. There were some skirmishes and detonations in the hills. On 1st August, the situation in the enclave was relatively quiet. UNPROFOR units in Zepa received the order to leave the pocket on the 2nd of August and reached Sarajevo on the next day." My question is this: Were UNPROFOR units in Zepa while you were observing the mining or blowing up of the mosque?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So was this before August [as interpreted] 31st, when they left Zepa?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: I don't know when they left Zepa nor do I know the day when the mosque was blown up, but I know that the UNPROFOR was there on that day and that they were advised -- cautioned to evacuate from there, to move to a safe area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. The reason I asked you about this is just to try to determine the sequence of events and the persons who were in Zepa at the time, because here it says that UNPROFOR left Zepa on 31st July. Now, my next question: After the 28th, when the evacuation in Zepa was over, was -- did anyone from the Main Staff remain in Zepa or were only people from the forward command post left there?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: After the fall of Zepa, there were only some troops from the Rogatica Brigade --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the other brigade.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] ... left in Zepa, but there was no one left from the Main Staff in Zepa after its fall.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, you just said that after the fall of Zepa, there was only some troops from the Rogatica Brigade, and I think you mentioned another unit. Can you repeat that, because the interpreters didn't catch that name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After the evacuation of the civilians and the fall of Zepa, only forces of the Rogatica Brigade and some members of the Visegrad Brigade remained in Zepa. Later on, I don't know whether that was five, seven, or ten days later, the forces from the Visegrad Brigade also departed from Zepa. And only a battalion of the Rogatica Brigade remained in Zepa, and that was the battalion that had already been on Zepa Mountain on the border-line between the Srebrenica and Rogatica municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this clarification. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Razdoljac, Mr. McCloskey, the Prosecutor, in his examination-in-chief, asked you whether there were any detainees in Zepa, in prison, and you said that you couldn't remember. And then he told you that there were some people who were held in detention there, and they testified. And he also showed you a list. Now, I would like to ask you about this detention. Were the detainees accessible to the representatives of the International Red Cross? In other words, was this an open-type detention facility where the ICRS [as interpreted] could have access?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Yes, I do know that it was open to visits by the ICRS [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean that no one from the Main Staff or any members of the Rogatica Brigade tried to conceal who was held in Rogatica? In view of the fact that this was an open-type facility, it was open to representatives of the International Red Cross, and they could visit them and be told by the detainees what was going on there? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Yes, I do, and it is certain that this detention facility in Rogatica was -- there were no attempts to conceal it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know whether some detainees did any work in Zepa? Can they form a sort of labour unit to collect certain raw materials and so on?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not familiar with that. I'm not familiar that there was any labour unit made up of detainees in Zepa to collect second-hand raw materials.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's request: Could the accused please repeat his question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm very sorry to stop both speakers. The interpreters have a big problem because you are overlapping. You should pause between question and answer. Otherwise, the interpreters will not catch it. Mr. Tolimir, could you please repeat your last question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. My apologies, both to the Chamber and the interpreters. I asked the witness whether it was his responsibility to know what other organs, who were not his subordinates, wrote about and reported, such as, for instance, Mr. Carkic, who was not a part of the Logistics Unit. So I would just like the witness to repeat his answer now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My answer is that I had no way of knowing that nor was it my responsibility to know what was going on or being done in the security organ. I received my orders only from the brigade commander that had to do with logistics, and I reported to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey showed you a document dated the 30th of July, signed by Captain Zoran Carkic, where, at the end of the document, he says -- and that was on the last page. He talks about various problems. That's in paragraph D, the last page of the document, and there he goes on to report or mention that some money was taken away from the detainees. And then he says by order of General Tolimir, he was to investigate this. So now I would like to ask you whether he could state that he was doing something according to my authority or under my authority if I was not even in Zepa on that day.

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Well, probably not. That's just perhaps his formulation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, does this here, then, perhaps relate to something that I said earlier? Because we see, from what it says there, that these Muslims had complained to General Tolimir - in other words, to me - and said that this was done by some men who were led by -- whose leader was a short man, Crni, and we see this document before us now that was the part that Mr. McCloskey referred you to. We see it now on our screens, and it says there: "Obviously -- it is obvious that this is Lieutenant Matic, who at the moment of separation of the Muslims, came to the spot and carried out searches in the school and at the school compound." And then the last sentence reads: "General Tolimir demands that this case be investigated and money found." Might this refer to his paragraph D and to the statement that he puts there, that I demanded that this be investigated and money found and returned?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your answers. Thank you for coming to testify here, and thank you for your decent conduct. I wish you a safe journey home. And thank you, Mr. President, as well as everyone who followed this testimony and my cross-examination. I have completed. I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Tolimir. Mr. McCloskey, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If I could have one minute, Mr. President. Mr. President, could we take the break a little early and let me see? I don't have much, but we -- but I'd like to be able to review the material and determine that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think this is a good proposal. We must have our second break now, and again the Court Usher will assist you during the break, sir. We will resume five minutes past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey, your re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Witness, on cross-examination, you, I think, clarified and reiterated to General Tolimir that you were involved in the logistics of getting vehicles for transporting people out of Zepa, and I want to just ask you a question or two about that. Do you know, was the main -- what would be the traditional chain of command for major orders like that, to get -- to get vehicles, bring them to an area, and move them out? Would that traditionally start as high as the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Well, it's logical that all operations and decisions be made first at the Main Staff, and that includes the decision to provide a large number of vehicles. It must have originated at the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, in chief, there was no mention -- sorry. In the cross-examination, there was no mention of procurement of vehicles. The witness was not asked about it. Now, who made the request for vehicles, that is something that must have happened during the talks which this witness attended.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, can you give any reference?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. In the time we have, I'm sure I could find it, but the witness clearly talked about and reiterated that he was getting -- he was doing his job of providing for transportation and doing the logistics, stating what his job was, and now I'm trying to give context to that, on where that came from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Was that during examination-in-chief or during cross?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It was cross. It was actually both. You remember, in examination, when I asked him what he was taking notes on, he said he was taking notes on getting ready on the 19th because they were about to reach an agreement. And then he, at least once, I think twice, answered a question, in response to the general, that what he was doing was organising and doing his logistics job. I mean, he must have repeated that more than once, because that's what he kept coming back to when he was asked to divert into other areas. I think -- I know it's late, but I specifically remember that, and I'm sorry I don't have the exact line and page. I can come up with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I can't assist you at the moment because I don't know where to find it. But perhaps Mr. Tolimir can help us. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, in my cross-examination, I only asked the witness about the last three issues. I didn't ask him anything about the evacuation, about the negotiations, or logistics. I only asked him about his stay in Zepa, the blowing up of the mosque, and the detention. About the purchase, under normal circumstances, of the vehicles for evacuation, I did not ask anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I've got the line. And I should stress it's not always the question, especially when it's a witness of the same organisation. It's the answer that I am referring to, and I can show you that it's on page 46. And line 15, he starts asking questions about when the activities in Zepa were finalised -- the question goes: "How -- let's start from the end, to make it easier for you. Do you know when the evacuation of Zepa was completed and when all the activities in Zepa were finalised?" Okay, this is a very broad two-part question, and it's the answer that I'm dealing with. The witness: "I said I don't know exactly when the evacuation was completed, but it took several days. I know what my task was within it, where I participated in securing 50 to 60 buses and lorries that carried the people being evacuated from Zepa and the support to the travel over bad roads towards Boksanica, and that involved the assistance from us, who were in Boksanica, and assistance from UNPROFOR. People moved over to buses, and then a convoy was formed which travelled, as far as I know, to Sarajevo." Now, this -- he says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think, Mr. McCloskey, this is a sufficient reference to a part of the cross-examination. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, sir, and I think you answered the question and said something to the effect that it would be natural for the Main Staff to be involved. And can you just remind us, how does the basic chain of command work? If the Main Staff wants something done, where does it send its orders to, normally? Where is the next basic unit or military organisation? And just very briefly.

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Well, the next step was the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And from the corps, it would then go to where?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: The brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me show you 65 ter 2254. And, again, with the help of the Usher, I can give you a -- well, it's one page. It's probably easier we just -- we just go there. And if we can blow it up, I'll look at the English. So we can see that this is from the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, Logistics Sector; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And it's to the 27th Logistic Base, as you've described where that fit in, and to the DK Command. And that's Drina Corps Command; correct?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that's to the assistant commander for logistics. All right. And I just look at the order, and it talks -- and we can see it --

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Yes, "PKPO," that's "Assistant Commander for Logistics."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And it's entitled "Order to transport of people and pull-out of war booty from Zepa." And we see, on that first page, it then goes on and says: "In order to transport people and collect and take war booty out of Zepa in an organised manner, I hereby issue the following:" And I won't go through the entire order, but it talks about -- can you read that first line: "The chief of -- " what service is that, under number 1?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: "Chief," and I can't make out, "Gr Sl."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think -- I'm sorry, it's small, but it's "GSVRS," which I think we know what that is. The word "obezbedice," something like that, what word is that?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: "Shall provide --" am I to read this aloud?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Actually, I just want to ask you: What is that service that you just described? What does it do, "obez" -- sorry, I can't pronounce it, "obezbedice"?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: "Shall secure," "shall send."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But what is this service? Is it a construction service, a transportation service, a security service? I'm just not sure of the English translation, so I'm just asking you, what does this word mean, "obezbedice"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think you misunderstood his answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it says -- as it continues, it reads ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Complete your answer, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says exactly what they will provide; one bus for transport at 1000 hours, 50 buses to transport people. That means that 51 buses, in total, should be supplied. Or if I may go back to what you just said, there was no talk here about procurement or purchase. General Tolimir said those were talks at Boksanica, where the representatives of the Muslim people agreed, and they wanted buses to be supplied. And my only duty was to provide buses available in my municipality. And my municipality, Rogatica, was a small town. It didn't have more than five buses, all in all, so we also involved the civilian presidency of the municipality to get co-operation from other municipalities in order to provide a sufficient number of buses; 50, 60.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for this answer. It was a long answer to a very short question. The question was related only to the word "obezbedice," if I understood you correctly, Mr. McCloskey, and that was already answered by the witness. That seems to be "shells secured" or "shells sent." It's not a unit, in my understanding, but you could clarify that with the witness again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. I think you're probably right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me ask you: It says: "The chief of the GrSl ..." What is "GrSl," if you remember?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: I don't know this abbreviation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And if we could just go to page 2 in the English, it should be -- and I just want to point out or ask you -- this is also to the 27th POB Command, also asking for vehicles. Can we look at the bottom of the original B/C/S. Unfortunately, it's been torn a bit, so we can't see any name. I don't know if you could help us. If we could just put up the B/C/S and blow it up a bit. We don't need the English for this. And go -- yeah, so we can get the whole bottom of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you read that last line, starting with "zamenik"?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: "Deputy assistant commander," and nothing else. The rest is missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Any idea who that might be from logistics of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: As far as I know, the deputy assistant commander for logistics was the late General Djukic. Sorry, the assistant commander for logistics was General Djukic. I don't know that he had a deputy assistant commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right, thank you. All right, let's now go to -- get a little bit closer to your brigade area. 65 ter 5279.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And as you'll see, we have here is the same date, the 19th of July. This one is from the commander, Major General Radislav Krstic, and it's from the Drina Corps Command. So this one is from Krstic, the commander of the Drina Corps. And does it appear to you to be on a similar subject, mobilisation of motor vehicles, a request, as we see, and it talks about the organised transport of the population from the former enclave of Zepa? So this is the same basic subject; correct?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Well, that's precisely as I said. The Main Staff would send to the lower command, that is to say, the corps command, their orders, and the corps sent it to the 27th Logistics Base and brigade commands, and the 27th Logistics Base sometimes sent orders directly to the assistant commander for logistics in various brigades. It sent orders directly, in other words, to the logistics organ of the brigades, except in this order from General Krstic, it lists what must be sent, broken down by municipalities; Vlasenica, Milici, Bratunac, Zvornik, Rogatica, Visegrad. It says exactly how many assets must be provided by each municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, yes, this is sent to the Ministry of Defence, among others, Rogatica. And I think, similarly to what you said, Rogatica had five buses and three freight trucks; is that about correct?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: This thing that was sent to the Ministries of Defence, that means the Ministry of Defence of Rogatica had to requisition these vehicles on the territory of the municipality; three buses and three freight trucks. That is to say, the Ministry of Defence had to issue a receipt when requisitioning a vehicle from a private owner.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, can you explain to us -- we can see, as you've just said, that this is not an order to the brigades here but that it's an order to the Ministry of Defence for Rogatica. Can you explain what the relationship is, and just briefly, between the Ministry of Defence organ at Rogatica and the army unit of Rogatica that you were part of?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Well, the Ministry of Defence was certainly part of the military defence of Rogatica, but the Ministry of Defence acted on the civilian level and it received requests for what needed to be mobilised and requisitioned; that is to say, recruits and equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay, and just one last little twist to this. The stamp in the lower left corner shows that it's a stamp from the Command of the 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade. This is now, of course, a VRS unit; correct?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you tell us what this 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade is familiarly known as, what city it's usually known as?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Sokolac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And we see that Sokolac is one of the Ministry of Defence people -- or units in this order. Do you recall whether or not you received this or something like it from the Drina Corps that engaged you in what you were talking about in your testimony earlier?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm just wondering. Do you recall getting an order -- a written order like this to engage you into getting buses and vehicles from Rogatica?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I'd like to offer both 2254 and 5279, these last two documents, into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: They will be received as exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Just for the record, I'd like to mention that 65 ter 02254 is received as Exhibit P01435, and 65 ter 05279 is received as Exhibit P01436. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, sir, I think we'll all remember that General Tolimir asked you or stated on cross-examination, in a question to you, that the prisoners at the Rogatica detention site were fully open to the ICRC, and I believe you agreed with him. And I want to show you a document, P00122, on that point. If we could blow it up so he'll have a chance to read it, and the same thing for us. And I'll try to briefly go over this. It's from the Main Staff of the VRS, Sector for Intel and Security, dated 29 July, "Very Urgent." And we see that it's to the IKM of the Drina Corps, personally to Krstic, Intelligence and Security of the Drina Corps, and then the Command of the 1st Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade. That's your brigade in Rogatica; correct?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And it says personally it's to your commander, Lieutenant-Colonel Rajko Kusic, and to Captain Pecanac. Who is Captain Pecanac?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Captain Pecanac was a member of the corps or the Main Staff. I'm not exactly sure. I don't know if he was the man in charge of security or morale, but he was -- he did not belong to my brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I'll try to briefly go over this, because there's only one section I really want to call to your attention. But we see it's entitled "Disarmament of the 1st Zepa Brigade," and it says: "On 28th of July, 1995, the Muslim side on several occasions, through UNPROFOR, asked for the --"

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: My apologies. Are you reading from the beginning or are you just reading another excerpt?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just from the beginning, starting: "Dana 28 ..."

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I think we can all read to ourselves that paragraph. It talks about the term of an agreement, signed on the 24th, regarding the disarmament of the brigade and the evacuation of its members, with UNPROFOR vehicles after exchange of prisoners that would be carried out in the whole territory, according to the principle "all for all." And then the next paragraph, it says: "In order to avoid being cheated by Muslims, the implementation of the cessation of fire was conditioned by liberation of all VRS members captured at Majevica, Lisaca and Vijenac." Then it goes on to talks about the surrender of UNPROFOR weapons and the disarmed members of the Zepa Brigade just to be kept at the UNPROFOR camp at Zepa until the exchange of prisoners. And then this paragraph is what I wanted to ask you about. It says: "Continue combat operations in order to surround and destroy the 1st Zepa Brigade until the Muslims make the exchange and carry out the agreement from 24 July related to their disarmament and surrender." And you're aware that at this -- at some point after the women and children were transported, the men in the army at Zepa were still fighting the VRS in the woods; correct?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Following the evacuation of women and children and all those who wanted to leave, armed troops, the Muslim Army, remained still in the area of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And is this what this paragraph is referring to?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: I don't know what it says here. I should read the whole paragraph. But what I do know is that after the civilians left, they continued to offer resistance, and there was also talk about some 800 to 900, 950, Zepa Brigade troops who crossed the Drina River and crossed over to the territory of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And it's -- and then it says: "Take all necessary measures to prevent them from leaving the encirclement." And then it says -- and I should point out that this is under the name of General Tolimir, as we'll get to the end. Then it says: "Do not register persons you capture before cessation of fire, and do not report them to international organisations. We are going to keep them for exchange in case the Muslims do not carry out the agreement or they manage to break through from the encirclement." Do you recall anyone -- did you hear any orders -- or did you receive any orders or did you even hear about any orders that you were not to register Muslim prisoners captured during these combat operations?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. During the cross-examination, we only talked about the prisoners of war who were already in detention facilities. But here, what is mentioned here are the prisoners or fighters who crossed over to the Republic of Serbia, and they didn't even surrender. So I would ask the Prosecutor to make the distinction. So what it says here is that they should not be registered until the cessation of fire, so the Prosecutor should make a distinction between what happened and what never happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I agree with the general that what he was talking about in cross was the -- he was suggesting the prisoners at Rogatica were fully registered and looked after. And what I'm showing here is, at the same time-frame, just a few kilometres away, General Tolimir is issuing instructions that when people get captured, they don't get registered. So this idea that they're registering people all the time is being contradicted. Clearly, the general's point about the Rogatica prison was that they were registering and treated them according to the Geneva Conventions. Well, as you know, I can test that, but I think it's perfectly fair for me to show, in the same neighbourhood, the same troops are capturing the same kind of men from the same unit and are specifically, for an unknown and unjustified reason, in my view, not registering them. It's precisely on point to what he is trying to argue. It's a different set of men. I agree with him on that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. If Mr. McCloskey is quoting something, then he should also quote the part where it says "until the cessation of fire." "Do not register them until the cessation of fire." You cannot take things out of context and quote just the portion -- some portions of the sentence and then skip some others. This is not here; there is no talk about any kind of registration. It's just the registration until the cessation of fire, and it says that they should be actually guarded until the exchange. So I don't know why he didn't mention that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, Mr. McCloskey has quoted exactly this part. That is on page 69, lines 5 to 8. Mr. McCloskey has quoted there, and I quote: "Do not register persons who capture before cessation of fire and do not report them to international organisations." And he quoted the next sentence as well. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. That is not the gist of my objection. My objection is to the question that was posed to the witness, where it wasn't said up until what moment they were not to be registered. There is -- that portion is missing from the question, "up until the cessation of the fire." The question was that they were asked not to register the prisoners of war. That was all that the question contained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Perhaps this is a translation issue, I am afraid. I think the meaning is absolutely the same: "Do not register persons who captured -- you capture before cessation of fire." This is the official translation we see in the English version of the B/C/S document, and Mr. McCloskey is not in a position to translate it himself in a different way. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's why I read that paragraph out completely. And so when I asked the question, it was clear, precisely, what I was referring to, not leaving out any of it. And I wanted to ask the witness, had he heard anything about not registering people. We can debate forever on what "cessation of fire" means, and I have no problem if the general brings that apart -- brings that in re-cross. "Cessation of fire" could be Dayton, it could be a lot of things. He could bring that out in cross. I don't have a problem with that. I just would like to ask this witness if he had heard of anything like this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, did you hear of any orders about not registering people, like this order or this -- sorry, before I say "order" -- before this -- as this document states?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: I neither heard nor received any orders that had anything to do with prisoners. And as I've already said earlier, that was not within my competence, anyway. Also, you claimed here that I said that the Red Cross was -- had a constant presence at the detention facility, but I only said that the Red Cross representatives could visit the detention facility whenever they chose, which is not to mean that they were there all the time, every single day. All I was trying to say was that there was no -- there was nothing to stop them from visiting the detention facility whenever they wanted to. That's what I was trying to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Have you heard Muslim complaints and testimony in other places that they were in that prison in Rogatica for months, without seeing the Red Cross, and were suffered to beatings and other abuses? Have you heard of that?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: No, I did not nor did I have any contact with the Muslims. And after the war, I met many of these one-time friends and we had coffee together or a chat, and never did any of them mention that they were mistreated at the prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you meet Mr. Hajric and Mr. Imamovic and Mr. Palic after the war?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: No, no. I've already said -- and what I said about after the war, I meant my neighbours and my co-workers. As for the people that you mentioned, they were neither my neighbours nor my co-workers, and I didn't even know them before the war or ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Have you heard about the mass grave at Vragolovi, right near Rogatica?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: I know where Vragolovi is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, all of this actually goes beyond the scope of my cross-examination, nor was it part of the examination-in-chief. So I don't know what foundation there is for this line of questioning, because if the Prosecutor had wanted to raise these issues, he could have done it during his examination-in-chief, but he did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. I did not want to have to raise another mass grave, but when he goes into and suggests that the ICRC was constantly at or available to the prisoners at the Rogatica prison, I certainly have a right to point out that three of those prisoners at the Rogatica prison were found -- where they were found. And I won't say anything more. But when he's suggesting the ICRC is involved in that, I certainly can contradict that and ask this person if he's ever heard of that or has knowledge of it, who, as you'll recall, agreed with him that the ICRC had access to it when they wanted to, as he reiterated is what he said in cross-examination, which I agree with him. He did say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would request that my colleague quote the witness's words the way he put them. The witness said that the prisoners were always accessible to the ICRS [as interpreted] representatives, not the other way around. Second, the witness knows nothing about the persons who were killed, which is what the Prosecutor asked him about, and he has no information as to where they were killed, and that was not the subject of the examination at all. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I have the impression that the last question is really far distinct of the line of questioning about a detention unit, and if it wasn't open -- a so-called open facility, open for visits of the Red Cross. I think this is -- your last question, taking into account what the witness testified about this prison, went really beyond the scope of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'll go on. To another subject, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That's a good idea. May I, at this point in time, recall the decision of the Chamber of the 20th of August for leave to amend the witness list and to add this witness to the witness list. That decision, on the request of the Prosecution, dealt with -- especially with Atlantida. We received some -- that means we received an answer of the witness that he doesn't know anything about Atlantida, but I think the main issue of the testimony of this witness should relate to that, so that we are now shifting slightly away from that. Perhaps you could focus on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think that's an important point, and I would like to address that just briefly, Mr. President; of course, not in the presence of the witness. I have one more short document and a very short mention of your concern that you've just talked about, so I think we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we go to P00487.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, sir, I think we'll all very clearly remember when General Tolimir put up the report of an analyst, Bezruchenko, from the OTP, that mentioned General Tolimir had said that Avdo Palic had provided information after -- about where the minefields were. And General Tolimir's point to you was very clearly that this was not a secret, this was open information, suggesting, I believe, that Bezruchenko knew about it and that the -- it was not a secret. But let's look at this document that is cited, I believe, by Bezruchenko, or certainly is right on point. And it's a document that we see is the name of Major General Zdravko Polimir." Can you tell me, did you ever hear of a Polimir, or is that another Zdravko, or is that just a typo, in your view?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: I've never heard of Polimir, but I cannot comment on the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you can comment on whether you think this is a typo, "General Major Zdravko Polimir." Do you think that's a typo, or can't you comment?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: What do you mean, whether it's a typo or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Well, it's possible to go either way. It could be a typo or maybe not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's look and see if this document -- you see the document and the typed version. Is this -- can you -- what kind of a machine was this typed on?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: What type of typewriter? What was the last thing you said?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is this a teletype?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when a teletype is sent out --

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- from -- and this is actually, as we can see, from the Command of the Rogatica Brigade, it goes out encrypted, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: That's how it should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we look up in the left-hand corner, and where it says "STR.POV," that means "Strictly Confidential Number"; correct?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that on 28 July 1995, when General Tolimir drafted this document and had it sent out, that this was a highly confidential document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if we're talking about documents, all wartime military documents have a designation "Strictly Confidential."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... explanations in front of the witness. It's improper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sorry, I have to stop this conversation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, I stopped you. Sorry, I stopped you. We can't continue in that way, that everybody is interrupting the other. Mr. Tolimir, if you want to raise an objection to the last document, you should raise your objection, but not give a statement, not give a statement, as you started to do on page 77, line 1 and 2. What is your objection?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My objection is this: This is an inappropriate witness to be asked about whether a strictly confidential document is accessible to a wider range of users or not based solely on the "Strictly Confidential" indication there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think this is not an objection with a foundation. Please carry on, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, you're an assistant commander for a very important brigade in the Drina Corps. Is this a confidential document?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: For logistics. Each of these documents, including my documents, where I was supposed to send meat or shoes or whatever supplies, they would all bear this indication "Strictly Confidential."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And they were all strictly confidential, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And they were very confidential military secret documents, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I mean, would you want the enemy or the press to know that you had received locations -- the exact locations of minefields in this context? It's pretty confidential stuff, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO RAZDOLJAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. I have nothing further, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, when I raised the concern in relation to the decision of the Chamber of the 20th of August in relation to Atlantida, you would like to address something, but in the absence of the witness. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, you will be pleased to hear that this concludes your examination, your testimony today. You are now free to return to your normal activities. The Chamber would like to thank you for your attendance here and for the answers you were able to provide. Thank you very much, again, and the Court Usher will assist you to leave the courtroom and to go back. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I'm sure the Court -- and I think you made reference to it. You will realise certain documents from what we have referred to as the Atlantida collection were coming in through evidence through Mr. Blaszczyk, and there was a very strong objection to those documents and their authenticity. And that was the basis for our motion to add this person on the witness list, because as you'll recall, Mr. Blaszczyk said that he -- his name was on a couple of the documents, and he was the assistant commander for logistics, and Mr. Blaszczyk felt that there was a good chance he would know something about that and be able to help us with that. And then you also know, because of the motion for subpoena, that we went to speak with him, and he chose not to speak with us. And so he received a court order and came here under a court order. And as I mentioned before he started, he came here this morning and was co-operative. Mr. Blaszczyk had a chance to speak to him very briefly as -- and then I spoke to him briefly afterward, and we learned from him that he didn't know anything about Atlantida but was able to provide information about some of the communications and other issues related to the Vila and who was at the Vila, which we put in the proofing note and gave it to the Defence as soon as we got it. The problem that we are faced with, when we have a witness that refuses to speak to us, which is his right, the only place that I can ask that he be ordered to answer questions is in this courtroom, and much of what you saw was an interview of the witness on key points. When he began speaking of cattle -- of taking cattle out of Zepa, I started asking him about the horse/pig farm from -- that we -- where we were all present, Sjemec. All that -- that's my only way of taking a witness, an assistant commander for logistics -- there's very few assistant commanders in a brigade. These are key people, they have key knowledge, and this was my chance to ask him questions about the key issues of the case. We got no objection on that, and I left it pretty limited within the two hours, and I kept it to the key issues. And I don't know -- it's a new area for us, it's a new area for me. It never happened before, where I'm interviewing a witness, in effect, before you. But I think the truth-seeking part of this Tribunal allows that, as you did, and I appreciate that. But I completely understand your point, but I wanted you to know the background, how it happened. There should not be surprise in these cases, but sometimes when you haven't had a chance to speak to someone, it's fair to ask the basic crucial questions associated. And, remember, Atlantida was a -- is filled with documents of all the key issues of the case. So if anything, that whole topic, even though he says he doesn't know about it, is a pretty big topic. So I hope I didn't go out of bounds on that, but I certainly acknowledge it was an issue. And one last thing: I apologise for interrupting like that, though when we start getting to key Main Staff witnesses and the general starts explaining, you know, his version of a document to the witness, as you know, that's just -- defeats the purpose of cross-examination. And I wanted to let the general know, to represent this case correctly, I have to object to him doing that. So I apologise for that ruckus, and I think you understand. And I will hopefully not have to do that again, because I know you will not like it and I will not like it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That's accepted, Mr. McCloskey, and I appreciate the additional information you were able to give to us about the background of this witness. And that will -- it's a kind of transparency also for the Defence and for the Chamber. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, we don't receive interpretation at the moment. I don't know what happened. Please repeat.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said I'm not interrupting the Prosecutor when he speaks, but I would appreciate it if he did not abuse redirect examination. In my cross, I did not say a word about Atlantida. The Prosecutor dealt with it in his examination-in-chief, and he got the answers he got. In future, I would appreciate it if questions in redirect would not be used for introducing new topics beyond the scope of cross-examination. I'm trying to be fair to all the parties, and I think this process should be fair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think after this exchange of positions, we all can agree that, up to now, the proceedings were, indeed, fair and co-operative, but sometimes there are issues in discussion, and this is not surprising, but we all should do our best to have a fair and expeditious trial. Thank you for your comments. I think both parties and the Chamber will do their utmost to have a good proceedings in the future again. We have to adjourn now. It is late again, and I apologise, on behalf of all participants, especially for the interpreters and the court recorder and the other staff members for this delay. We adjourn and resume tomorrow, in the afternoon, quarter past two, in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 1st day of December, 2010, at 2.15 p.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.11 p.m.,
